title: Makkah under pressure
subtitle: From the public call to the return from al-Ṭāʾif: how Makkah became a city the Prophet ﷺ could no longer live in

units.title: The call made public
units.kicker: The message leaves the private circle

when.label: c. 613 CE, about three years after the first revelation

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq reports that men and women entered Islam in groups until it was talked about across Makkah. Then Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to proclaim openly what had come to him and to call people to it.
He puts three years between the start of the mission and this command, but only with the hedge 'as it reached me'.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq hedges the three-year interval (fīmā balaghanī); no chain is given.

statements.text: The verses Ibn Isḥāq gives for the command include the order to proclaim what he was commanded and to warn his nearest kin.

Al-Bukhārī's report from Ibn ʿAbbās says that when the verse on warning the nearest kin came, the Prophet ﷺ climbed al-Ṣafā and called out to the clans of Quraysh, and Abū Lahab answered him with a curse.

Ibn Isḥāq reports, with the hedge 'as it reached me', that his people did not turn away from him until he spoke of their gods and found fault with them. After that they united in hostility, apart from the few Muslims, who kept themselves hidden.
His uncle Abū Ṭālib took his side, protected him and stood in front of him, and would not hand him over.
Leading men of Quraysh went to Abū Ṭālib to complain, among them ʿUtba and Shayba, sons of Rabīʿa, Abū Sufyān b. Ḥarb, Abū al-Bakhtarī, Abū Jahl, al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra and al-ʿĀṣ b. Wāʾil.

When Abū Ṭālib asked him not to load him with more than he could bear, the Prophet ﷺ replied that even if they put the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left he would not give up the matter until Allah made it prevail or he perished in it. Abū Ṭālib then told him to go and say what he wished, for he would never hand him over.

quran.gist: The Prophet is told to declare openly what he has been commanded and to turn away from those who set up partners with Allah.
quran.context: Ibn Isḥāq cites it as the command that ended the private phase of the call (S0367).

quran.gist: He is told to warn his own closest relatives first.
quran.context: Cited by Ibn Isḥāq (S0367); al-Bukhārī 4770 ties it to the call from al-Ṣafā.

people.name: Abū Ṭālib b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib
people.who: The Prophet's paternal uncle, head of Banū Hāshim
people.here: Refused to hand his nephew over

people.name: Abū Lahab
people.who: Another paternal uncle
people.here: Answered the call at al-Ṣafā with a curse

reveal.text: The Kaʿba stands in the bed of a narrow valley closed in by bare, rocky hills, so the town's open space was small and everyone met around the sanctuary.

question.q: According to Ibn Isḥāq, what turned Quraysh from indifference to open hostility?

options.text: He spoke of their gods and found fault with them
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq says they did not turn away from him until he did this.
No source here says this; the complaint was about their gods and their fathers' religion.

options.text: He left Makkah for another town
options.why: He stayed; Abū Ṭālib protected him in Makkah.

units.matters: Once the call was public, everything depended on the protection of one uncle. That single thread of protection is what the rest of this act tests.

units.title: Hands on him at the Ḥijr
units.kicker: Hostility at the sanctuary and at home

lights.name: the nobles of Quraysh in the Ḥijr

statements.text: Asked about the worst he saw Quraysh do to the Prophet ﷺ, ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ described their nobles gathered in the Ḥijr, complaining that he had mocked their judgement, insulted their fathers, faulted their religion, split their community and reviled their gods.
As the Prophet ﷺ passed them three times while circling the House, they made remarks at him. At the third pass he stopped and spoke to them, and they fell silent.

The next day they surrounded him together and one of them seized him by the folds of his cloak. Abū Bakr stood between them, weeping, and asked whether they would kill a man for saying 'My Lord is Allah'.
In al-Bukhārī's version the attacker was ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, who twisted a garment around the Prophet's ﷺ neck while he prayed in the Ḥijr.

Another report in al-Bukhārī says that while the Prophet ﷺ was prostrating at the Kaʿba, ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, urged on by a group of Quraysh, laid the afterbirth of a slaughtered camel on his back, and his daughter Fāṭima came and removed it.
Ibn Isḥāq names the neighbours who harassed him at his house: Abū Lahab, al-Ḥakam b. Abī al-ʿĀṣ, ʿUqba b. Abī Muʿayṭ, ʿAdī b. Ḥamrāʾ al-Thaqafī and Ibn al-Aṣdāʾ al-Hudhalī.

He reports, with the hedge 'as was mentioned to me', that one of them threw a sheep's womb on him while he prayed and another threw it into his cooking pot, so that he set up a stone to screen himself when praying.
statements.note: Hedged by Ibn Isḥāq (fīmā dhukira lī); no chain.

statements.text: Through ʿUrwa b. al-Zubayr he adds that the Prophet ﷺ would carry the filth out on a stick, stand at his door, ask the clan of ʿAbd Manāf what sort of neighbourliness this was, and throw it into the road.

quran.gist: A believing man of Pharaoh's people asks them whether they would kill a man only because he says his Lord is Allah, when he has brought them clear signs.
quran.context: Abū Bakr's words at the Ḥijr are the words of this verse; al-Bukhārī 3856 has him say them.

people.name: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ
people.who: Companion, son of ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ
people.here: The witness of the Ḥijr incident

people.name: Fāṭima
people.who: The Prophet's daughter
people.here: Removed the filth from his back

reveal.text: The Ḥijr is the curved, open enclosure on the north-west side of the Kaʿba, where people sat in the shade of the House.

question.q: Quraysh have surrounded him in the Ḥijr and one has grabbed his cloak. Who steps in?

options.why: Both Ibn Isḥāq and al-Bukhārī say Abū Bakr pushed in and spoke the words of 40:28.
Abū Ṭālib protected him through his clan, but he is not named in this incident.
Ḥamza is not named in either account of this incident.

units.matters: Even under Abū Ṭālib's protection, the Prophet ﷺ could be mobbed at the sanctuary and insulted in his own home. The protection kept him alive; it did not keep him safe.

units.title: The weak in the noon heat
units.kicker: Those with no clan to shield them

statements.text: Bilāl b. Rabāḥ was a slave born among Banū Jumaḥ. When the noon heat was at its height Umayya b. Khalaf would take him out, lay him on his back on the stony valley floor of Makkah and have a great rock placed on his chest.
Umayya told him it would go on until he died or rejected Muḥammad and worshipped al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā. Bilāl kept repeating 'One, One' (aḥad, aḥad).

Abū Bakr, whose house was among Banū Jumaḥ, gave Umayya a stronger slave of his own in exchange for Bilāl and freed him. Ibn Isḥāq lists six others he freed for their Islam, among them ʿĀmir b. Fuhayra and Zinnīra.
Banū Makhzūm took ʿAmmār b. Yāsir out with his father and mother, a household of Muslims, and tormented them on the scorching ground. They killed his mother, who refused to give up Islam.
Ibn Isḥāq reports, with the hedge 'as it reached me', that the Prophet ﷺ passed them and told the family of Yāsir to be patient, for their promised meeting place was Paradise.
statements.note: Hedged by Ibn Isḥāq (fīmā balaghanī); no chain.

statements.text: Saʿīd b. Jubayr asked Ibn ʿAbbās whether the torture was bad enough to excuse giving up the religion. He said yes: some were beaten, starved and kept thirsty until they could not sit upright, and then said whatever their tormentors demanded.

discover.label: Feel the valley floor at noon

reveal.text: Makkah's valley floor is gravel and sand between bare rock hills. In the hot months, temperatures in the middle of the day often pass 40 °C and the ground is hotter still.

question.q: Ibn ʿAbbās said some believers gave in under torture. What does that tell you about the pressure on those without a protector?

options.text: Faith alone could not stop the beatings; only protection or escape could
options.why: Abū Bakr's purchases and the later move to Abyssinia were the two ways out the sources describe.

options.text: The clan system protected only those who belonged to a strong clan
options.why: Slaves like Bilāl and clients like Yāsir's family had no one to stand in front of them.

units.matters: Abū Ṭālib could shield his nephew, but nobody shielded the slaves and the clientless. Their suffering is the first reason a place of refuge was needed.

units.title: A land of truthfulness

when.label: Rajab, fifth year of the mission (c. 615 CE)

place.note: The kingdom of Abyssinia (Aksum), across the Red Sea; not drawn on this map

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq says that when the Prophet ﷺ saw what his companions suffered, while he himself was kept safe by his standing with Allah and with Abū Ṭālib, and that he could not protect them, he told them to go to Abyssinia.
He described it as a land with a king under whom no one is wronged, a land of truthfulness, where they could stay until Allah gave them a way out.
They left for fear of being forced from their religion, fleeing to Allah with their faith. Ibn Isḥāq calls this the first emigration in Islam.

Among the first to go were ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān with his wife Ruqayya, the Prophet's ﷺ daughter; Abū Ḥudhayfa b. ʿUtba with Sahla bint Suhayl; al-Zubayr b. al-ʿAwwām; Muṣʿab b. ʿUmayr; ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf; Abū Salama with Umm Salama; and ʿUthmān b. Maẓʿūn.
Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib, the Prophet's ﷺ cousin, went with his wife, and their son ʿAbd Allāh was born in Abyssinia.
Ibn Isḥāq counts all who reached Abyssinia, not counting their children, as eighty-three men, if ʿAmmār b. Yāsir was among them, which he doubts.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq himself is unsure whether ʿAmmār went; the total depends on it.

statements.text: Ibn Saʿd dates the first departure to Rajab of the fifth year of the mission.

sources.note: Account of the first emigration to Abyssinia

statements.text: To reach Abyssinia from Makkah the emigrants had to reach the Red Sea coast, roughly 70 km to the west, and cross by boat to the African shore.
statements.basis: approximate map distance; the port is not in the gazetteer

people.name: ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān and Ruqayya
people.who: Companion of Banū Umayya and the Prophet's daughter
people.here: Named first among the emigrants

people.name: Jaʿfar b. Abī Ṭālib
people.who: The Prophet's cousin, brother of ʿAlī
people.here: Emigrated with his wife

reveal.text: The Red Sea separates the Ḥijāz from the African coast; at this latitude it is roughly 300 km wide.

question.q: His companions are being tortured and he cannot stop it. Where does the Prophet ﷺ tell them to go?

options.why: Ibn Isḥāq gives his words about a king under whom no one is wronged.
Yathrib comes later, after the pledges at al-ʿAqaba; it was not yet an option.
The approach to al-Ṭāʾif came years later, and he went himself.

units.matters: The first emigration was a hijra in all but destination: leaving home and kin to keep one's religion. It showed that refuge outside Makkah was possible.

units.title: Before the Najāshī

place.note: The Najāshī's court; site not located on this map

lights.name: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ and ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Rabīʿa

statements.text: When Quraysh saw that the emigrants had found safety and a settled home, they sent two hardy men, ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Rabīʿa and ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, with gifts for the Najāshī and his generals, to have them handed back.
Ibn Isḥāq's account of what followed is told by Umm Salama, who was among the emigrants.
Summoned by the king, the emigrants agreed among themselves to say only what they knew and what their Prophet ﷺ had commanded, whatever the outcome.

Jaʿfar spoke for them. He said they had worshipped idols, eaten carrion, cut family ties, wronged their neighbours and let the strong devour the weak, until a messenger from among them, whose lineage and honesty they knew, called them to worship Allah alone, to speak truthfully, keep trusts and honour kinship.

He told the king that their own people had tortured them to force them back to idols, and that when they were overpowered and hemmed in they chose his land and his protection, hoping not to be wronged there.
Asked for something of the revelation, Jaʿfar recited the opening of Sūrat Maryam. Umm Salama says the Najāshī and his bishops wept, and the king refused to hand the emigrants over.

quran.gist: Sūrat Maryam opens with Zakariyyā's prayer for a son and goes on to tell of Maryam and the birth of ʿĪsā.
quran.context: Umm Salama's report in Ibn Isḥāq says Jaʿfar recited its opening before the Najāshī (S0462).

people.name: Umm Salama bint Abī Umayya
people.who: Emigrant with her husband Abū Salama; later a wife of the Prophet
people.here: The narrator of the scene

people.name: ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ
people.who: Envoy of Quraysh, later a Companion
people.here: Came to have the emigrants returned

discover.label: Hear what Jaʿfar said they fled from

reveal.text: Jaʿfar's own words name the reason for leaving: their people tortured them, pressed them and came between them and their religion.

question.q: What did Jaʿfar recite when the Najāshī asked to hear the revelation?

options.why: Umm Salama's account says so.
Not in the account.
Not in the account.

units.matters: Quraysh's reach extended across the sea, but a just ruler outside their power could refuse them. Protection, not distance, was what made a refuge.

units.title: Only under someone's protection
units.kicker: Returning emigrants and Abū Bakr's attempt to leave

statements.text: Word reached the emigrants in Abyssinia that the people of Makkah had become Muslim, and some set out for home. Near Makkah they learned the report was false.
None of them entered except under a protector's guarantee (jiwār) or in hiding. Ibn Isḥāq counts thirty-three men who came back from Abyssinia to Makkah.
ʿUthmān b. Maẓʿūn entered under the protection of al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra, and Abū Salama under that of his maternal uncle Abū Ṭālib.

Abū Bakr, when Makkah had become narrow for him and he was harmed there, asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to emigrate and set out. After a day or two on the road he met Ibn al-Daghina, chief of the Aḥābīsh.
Ibn al-Daghina said a man who supported his kin, helped in misfortune and did good should not be driven out. He brought Abū Bakr back and announced to Quraysh that he was under his protection.
Abū Bakr prayed at a place of prayer by his door and wept as he recited. Women, children and slaves stopped to watch, and Quraysh complained that he would turn them.

Told to worship only inside his house, Abū Bakr gave the protection back, saying he was content with the protection of Allah. Soon after, a man of Quraysh threw dust on his head on his way to the Kaʿba.

people.name: Ibn al-Daghina
people.who: Chief of the Aḥābīsh, the allied tribes below Makkah
people.here: Brought Abū Bakr back under his protection

people.name: ʿUthmān b. Maẓʿūn
people.who: Early emigrant of Banū Jumaḥ
people.here: Re-entered Makkah under al-Walīd's protection

discover.label: Where Abū Bakr was turned back

reveal.text: In al-Bukhārī's version Abū Bakr had reached Bark al-Ghimād when Ibn al-Daghina met him. The place is not securely located, so it is not drawn.

question.q: Why did Quraysh object to Abū Bakr praying by his door?

options.text: They feared their women, children and weaker folk would be drawn in
options.why: That is the complaint they took to Ibn al-Daghina.
The sources give no such complaint.

options.text: He prayed facing away from the Kaʿba
options.why: The sources give no such complaint.

units.matters: By now a Muslim could live in Makkah only on a non-Muslim's guarantee, and even the most respected of them had tried to leave. Makkah was becoming a city one could enter but not live in.

units.title: The document in the Kaʿba
units.kicker: Quraysh boycott Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib

place.note: The ravine of Abū Ṭālib in Makkah; exact site not established

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq gives the background: the companions had found safety in Abyssinia, the Najāshī had protected them, ʿUmar had become Muslim and stood with Ḥamza beside the Prophet ﷺ, and Islam was spreading among the tribes.
Quraysh agreed in writing against Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib: no one would marry their women or give women to them in marriage, sell them anything or buy anything from them.
They hung the sheet inside the Kaʿba to bind themselves the more firmly.
Ibn Isḥāq names the scribe as Manṣūr b. ʿIkrima of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār; Ibn Hishām adds, with 'it is said', that it was al-Naḍr b. al-Ḥārith.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq and Ibn Hishām name different scribes.

statements.text: The two clans gathered with Abū Ṭālib in his ravine (shiʿb). Of Banū Hāshim only Abū Lahab left them and sided with Quraysh.
Ibn Isḥāq reports that Abū Lahab met Hind bint ʿUtba and asked whether he had not stood by al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā; she thanked him for it.
Ibn Saʿd dates the start of the boycott to Muḥarram of the seventh year of the mission; later writers usually give its length as two or three years.

sources.note: Account of the ṣaḥīfa and the shiʿb

statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq's text here gives no length; other sources differ between two and three years.

quran.gist: Abū Lahab's efforts, and Abū Lahab himself, are ruined.
quran.context: Ibn Isḥāq ties it to Abū Lahab's mockery of the promise of the hereafter (S0476); al-Bukhārī 4770 ties it to his curse at al-Ṣafā. The occasion is disputed; that it concerns Abū Lahab is not.

people.name: Abū Lahab (ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib)
people.who: The Prophet's uncle
people.here: The one Hāshimite who joined the boycott

people.name: Manṣūr b. ʿIkrima
people.who: Of Banū ʿAbd al-Dār
people.here: Named by Ibn Isḥāq as the scribe

reveal.text: Makkah's shiʿāb are narrow side valleys that run up from the main valley into the hills. A clan could be shut into one with a single entrance.

question.q: Quraysh have sealed the boycott. Which member of the Prophet's ﷺ own clan goes over to them?

options.why: Ibn Isḥāq says he alone of Banū Hāshim left and backed Quraysh.
Not named as leaving.
He led the clans into his ravine.

units.matters: The boycott turned the quarrel from individuals to whole clans: the Prophet's ﷺ kin were cut off from trade and marriage for refusing to give him up.

units.title: Camels in the night

place.note: Khaṭm al-Ḥajūn, in upper Makkah; exact spot not established

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq reports, with the hedge 'as it reached me', that Hishām b. ʿAmr would lead a camel loaded with food to the mouth of the ravine at night, slip off its halter and drive it in to the besieged clans, and later did the same with cloth.

Hishām asked Zuhayr b. Abī Umayya, whose mother was ʿĀtika bint ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, whether he could eat, dress and marry while his mother's kin could neither buy nor sell. Zuhayr said he was only one man; Hishām said he had found a second, himself.
They won over al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī, then Abū al-Bakhtarī and Zamʿa b. al-Aswad. The five met at night at Khaṭm al-Ḥajūn in upper Makkah and swore to see the document torn up.
In the morning Zuhayr circled the Kaʿba seven times and asked the people of Makkah whether they should eat and dress while Banū Hāshim perished, unable to trade.
Abū Jahl objected; Zamʿa, Abū al-Bakhtarī, al-Muṭʿim and Hishām each disowned the document. Abū Jahl said it had been settled by night somewhere else.
When al-Muṭʿim went to tear it up, he found termites had eaten it, except the words 'In Your name, O Allah'.

Ibn Hishām adds, from 'some people of knowledge', that the Prophet ﷺ had told Abū Ṭālib that the termites had left only the name of Allah, and that Abū Ṭālib put this to Quraysh as a test, which only hardened them.
statements.note: Unnamed authorities; it also differs from Ibn Isḥāq on what was left of the sheet.

people.name: Hishām b. ʿAmr
people.who: Of Banū ʿĀmir b. Luʾayy, related to Banū Hāshim through his mother's side
people.here: Fed the clans and organised the five

people.name: al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī
people.who: Chief of Banū Nawfal; did not become Muslim
people.here: One of the five; found the document eaten

reveal.text: Ibn Isḥāq places Khaṭm al-Ḥajūn, where the five met, in the upper part of Makkah.

question.q: Who found that termites had eaten the document?

options.why: He went to tear it up and found it eaten.
He defended the document.
He was sitting at the side of the Mosque in Ibn Isḥāq's account.

units.matters: The boycott ended through kinship and conscience among non-Muslims, not through any change of heart in Quraysh as a whole. Remember al-Muṭʿim's name.

units.title: At Abū Ṭālib's bedside

when.label: c. 619 CE, three years before the Hijra

statements.text: When Abū Ṭālib fell ill, Quraysh said among themselves that Ḥamza and ʿUmar had become Muslim and Muḥammad's cause had spread through all their clans, so they should secure terms through Abū Ṭālib.

Through Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Isḥāq names those who came: ʿUtba and Shayba, sons of Rabīʿa, Abū Jahl, Umayya b. Khalaf and Abū Sufyān. They proposed that he leave them their religion and they would leave him his.
The Prophet ﷺ asked them for a single word by which they would rule the Arabs and the non-Arabs would follow them: to say there is no god but Allah and give up what they worshipped besides Him.
They clapped their hands, asked whether he would make the gods one God, and left resolved to keep the religion of their fathers. Ibn Isḥāq says the opening of Sūrat Ṣād was revealed about them.

In Ibn Isḥāq's version Abū Ṭālib said he would have said the word were it not that Quraysh would think he said it from fear of death. As he was dying al-ʿAbbās saw his lips moving and said he had said it; the Prophet ﷺ answered, 'I did not hear it.'
statements.note: The chain includes an unnamed member of al-ʿAbbās's family, and al-Bukhārī's report gives a different ending.

statements.text: In al-Bukhārī's report from al-Musayyab b. Ḥazn, the Prophet ﷺ urged him at his death with Abū Jahl and ʿAbd Allāh b. Abī Umayya present. They asked whether he would leave the religion of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and his last words were that he held to it.

In the same report the Prophet ﷺ said he would ask forgiveness for him unless he was forbidden, and verses were then revealed on not seeking forgiveness for idolaters and on Allah alone guiding whom He wills.

quran.gist: The unbelievers express astonishment that he has made the many gods into one God.
quran.context: Ibn Isḥāq says the opening of Sūrat Ṣād came down about the delegation at Abū Ṭālib's bedside (S0586).

quran.gist: The Prophet cannot guide whomever he loves; it is Allah who guides whom He wills.
quran.context: Al-Bukhārī 3884 links it to Abū Ṭālib's death.

people.name: al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib
people.who: The Prophet's uncle, not yet Muslim
people.here: Claimed to hear Abū Ṭālib's last words, in Ibn Isḥāq's version

question.q: Ibn Isḥāq and al-Bukhārī tell the end of Abū Ṭālib differently. Which account carries more weight, and why?

options.text: Al-Bukhārī's, because its chain is fully named and rigorously checked
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq's chain contains an unnamed link; al-Bukhārī's is graded ṣaḥīḥ.

options.text: Both agree on what matters for this story: the protector was dying
options.why: Either way, the shield around the Prophet ﷺ was about to be lost.

units.matters: Abū Ṭālib protected his nephew for years without accepting his message. With his death the clan's protection, not the message, was what came to an end.

units.title: Two losses in one year
units.kicker: The deaths of Khadīja and Abū Ṭālib, the 'Year of Sorrow' of later writers

when.label: c. 619 CE, three years before the Hijra

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq says Khadīja bint Khuwaylid and Abū Ṭālib died in the same year, and that misfortunes then came one after another upon the Prophet ﷺ.
He describes Khadīja as a true support to him in Islam, someone to whom he would confide his troubles.
He describes Abū Ṭālib as his support and stronghold, his defence and helper against his own people.
Both Ibn Isḥāq and a report from ʿUrwa in al-Bukhārī place Khadīja's death three years before the Prophet ﷺ left for Madina.
Al-Bukhārī reports that Jibrīl told the Prophet ﷺ to greet Khadīja with peace from her Lord and to give her news of a house in Paradise made of hollow pearl, with no noise and no toil.
After Abū Ṭālib died, Quraysh did to the Prophet ﷺ harm they had not hoped to do while his uncle lived, until a lout of Quraysh blocked his way and threw dust on his head.
Through ʿUrwa b. al-Zubayr, Ibn Isḥāq reports that he went home with the dust still on his head, and one of his daughters washed it off, weeping.
He told her not to weep, for Allah would protect her father.
In the same report he said that Quraysh had done nothing to him that he hated until Abū Ṭālib died.

people.name: Khadīja bint Khuwaylid
people.who: The Prophet's wife and the first to believe in him
people.here: Died about three years before the Hijra

people.name: Abū Ṭālib
people.who: His uncle and protector
people.here: Died in the same year

reveal.text: Seventh-century Makkah filled a valley only a few kilometres long; in so small a town there was no avoiding one's opponents.

question.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ say to his daughter as she washed the dust away?

options.text: Do not weep, for Allah will protect your father
options.why: Reported by ʿUrwa through Ibn Isḥāq.
No such words are reported.

units.matters: One loss took his closest companion at home, the other his protection in public. His own words mark the turning point: Makkah without Abū Ṭālib was a different city.

units.title: Alone to al-Ṭāʾif

when.label: Shawwāl, tenth year of the mission (619 CE)

lights.name: ʿAbd Yālīl, Masʿūd and Ḥabīb, sons of ʿAmr

statements.text: With the harm increasing, the Prophet ﷺ went to al-Ṭāʾif seeking help and protection from Thaqīf against his own people, and hoping they would accept what he brought from Allah.
Ibn Isḥāq says he went alone; Ibn Saʿd reports that Zayd b. Ḥāritha went with him.

sources.note: Account of the journey to al-Ṭāʾif

statements.note: The sources differ on whether Zayd b. Ḥāritha accompanied him.

statements.text: Ibn Saʿd dates the journey to Shawwāl of the tenth year of the mission.

sources.note: Account of the journey to al-Ṭāʾif

statements.text: He went to three brothers who were then the chiefs of Thaqīf: ʿAbd Yālīl, Masʿūd and Ḥabīb, sons of ʿAmr b. ʿUmayr. One of them had a wife of Quraysh from Banū Jumaḥ.
He called them to Allah and asked them to stand with him against those of his people who opposed him.

All three refused. One said he would tear the covering of the Kaʿba if Allah had sent him; another asked whether Allah could find no one else to send; the third said he would never speak to him at all.
Ibn Isḥāq reports, with the hedge 'as was mentioned to me', that he asked them to keep the matter to themselves, not wanting his people to hear of it and be emboldened against him.
statements.note: Hedged by Ibn Isḥāq (fīmā dhukira lī).

statements.text: Al-Ṭāʾif lies about 64 km in a straight line east-south-east of Makkah, on a plateau well over a thousand metres higher, reached by climbing the escarpment.
statements.basis: computed distance between gazetteer points; terrain data

people.name: ʿAbd Yālīl b. ʿAmr
people.who: One of the three chiefs of Thaqīf
people.here: Refused him

people.name: Zayd b. Ḥāritha
people.who: The Prophet's freed slave and adopted son
people.here: Named as his companion by Ibn Saʿd, not by Ibn Isḥāq

reveal.text: Between the two towns the land rises from the low Makkan valleys to the cooler highland where al-Ṭāʾif sits among orchards and vineyards.

question.q: What did the Prophet ﷺ ask of the chiefs of Thaqīf?

options.text: Acceptance of his message and protection against his own people
options.why: Ibn Isḥāq says he sought nuṣra and protection from Thaqīf.

options.text: A place for the Muslims of Abyssinia to settle
options.why: Not in the account.
Not in the account.

units.matters: This was the first time the Prophet ﷺ himself sought a protector outside Makkah. The question 'who will shelter us?' had become the question of his mission.

units.title: In the shade of a vine

when.label: During the visit to al-Ṭāʾif (619 CE)

place.note: A walled garden of ʿUtba and Shayba, sons of Rabīʿa

lights.name: ʿUtba and Shayba, sons of Rabīʿa
the louts and slaves of al-Ṭāʾif

statements.text: Thaqīf set their louts and slaves on him, cursing and shouting, until a crowd gathered and drove him into a walled garden of ʿUtba and Shayba, sons of Rabīʿa, who were inside.
He sat in the shade of a grapevine while the two sons of Rabīʿa watched.

Ibn Isḥāq reports, with the hedge 'as was mentioned to me', a prayer he made there: complaining to Allah of his weakness, his lack of means and his lowliness before people, asking to whom Allah would hand him over, and saying that if Allah was not angry with him, he did not mind.
statements.note: Ibn Isḥāq gives no chain (fīmā dhukira lī); the other versions of this prayer are judged weak by some ḥadīth critics.

statements.text: Moved by kinship, the sons of Rabīʿa sent their Christian slave ʿAddās with a bunch of grapes on a plate.
The Prophet ﷺ said 'In the name of Allah' before eating. ʿAddās remarked that people of this land did not say that, and said he was a Christian from Nineveh.
When the Prophet ﷺ called Nineveh the town of the righteous man Yūnus b. Mattā, and said Yūnus was his brother, a prophet as he was, ʿAddās bent over him and kissed his head, hands and feet.
The brothers warned ʿAddās not to let the man turn him from his religion; ʿAddās answered that nothing on earth was better than this man.

ʿĀʾisha reports that when she asked whether he had faced a day harder than Uḥud, the Prophet ﷺ spoke of the day he presented himself to Ibn ʿAbd Yālīl and was refused. He walked on, distressed, and came to himself only at Qarn al-Thaʿālib, where the angel of the mountains offered to crush them between the two mountains; he answered that he hoped their descendants would worship Allah alone.

people.name: ʿAddās
people.who: Christian slave of the sons of Rabīʿa, from Nineveh
people.here: Brought the grapes and kissed the Prophet's head, hands and feet

people.name: Ibn ʿAbd Yālīl b. ʿAbd Kulāl
people.who: The chief named in al-Bukhārī's report
people.here: Ibn Isḥāq names the chiefs as sons of ʿAmr b. ʿUmayr; the naming differs between the sources

reveal.text: Qarn al-Thaʿālib, where he came to himself, lay on his way back toward Makkah. Later commentators identify it with Qarn al-Manāzil, the mīqāt for the people of Najd; it is not drawn here.
reveal.note: The identification with Qarn al-Manāzil is by later commentators, not in the ḥadīth itself.

question.q: A stranger in a hostile town is offered grapes by a Christian slave. What will the slave learn from him?

options.text: That he knows of Yūnus b. Mattā of Nineveh and calls him a brother prophet
options.why: That is the exchange Ibn Isḥāq records.

options.text: That the sons of Rabīʿa will protect him
options.why: They did not; they warned ʿAddās against him.

units.matters: The worst day of rejection held a single welcome, from a slave far from home. In his own telling the Prophet ﷺ chose hope for Thaqīf's descendants over revenge.

units.title: Night prayer at Nakhla
units.kicker: On the road back to Makkah

place.note: Nakhla, a valley between al-Ṭāʾif and Makkah; not drawn on this map

statements.text: Having given up hope of any good from Thaqīf, the Prophet ﷺ turned back toward Makkah. At Nakhla he rose in the depth of the night to pray.
The Qurʾān tells of a band of jinn who listened to the Qurʾān and went back to their people as warners, having believed.
Ibn Isḥāq places that listening on this night at Nakhla, after al-Ṭāʾif.
statements.note: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Bukhārī places the jinn's listening at Nakhla during a dawn prayer, with companions, on the way to the market of ʿUkāẓ, not on the return from al-Ṭāʾif.

statements.text: Ibn Isḥāq says, with the hedge 'as was mentioned to me', that they were seven jinn of Naṣībīn.
statements.note: Hedged by Ibn Isḥāq (fīmā dhukira lī).

statements.text: He says Allah then told the Prophet ﷺ their story in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf and in Sūrat al-Jinn.
Away from any town, the night sky over the Ḥijāz hills is very dark and the air cools quickly after sunset.

quran.gist: A group of jinn was turned toward the Prophet to hear the Qurʾān; they told one another to listen in silence, then went back to warn their people.
quran.context: Ibn Isḥāq quotes it for the night at Nakhla (S0591); the occasion is disputed.

quran.gist: The Prophet is told to say it has been revealed to him that a band of jinn listened and found the recitation wondrous.

question.q: Rejected by Thaqīf, the Prophet ﷺ prays alone at night and the Qurʾān tells of listeners he could not see. What does the placing of this story after al-Ṭāʾif suggest?

options.text: That rejection by people did not mean the message had no hearers
options.why: This is the reading Ibn Isḥāq's arrangement invites; note that al-Bukhārī places the event differently.

units.matters: Whatever its exact date, Ibn Isḥāq set this story at the low point of the journey. It moves the story from what the Prophet ﷺ lost to what he still had.

units.title: Entering Makkah under al-Muṭʿim
units.kicker: A protector who was not a Muslim

lights.name: al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī and his sons

statements.text: Ibn Hishām explains a line in Ḥassān b. Thābit's elegy for al-Muṭʿim, 'you gave protection to the Messenger of Allah', with this account; he gives no chain for it.

When the people of al-Ṭāʾif refused him, the Prophet ﷺ went to Ḥirāʾ and sent to al-Akhnas b. Sharīq asking for protection. Al-Akhnas declined, saying he was a confederate and a confederate cannot grant protection.
He then sent to Suhayl b. ʿAmr, who declined, saying Banū ʿĀmir do not give protection against Banū Kaʿb.
Al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī agreed. He and his household armed themselves, went to the Mosque, and sent word for the Prophet ﷺ to enter.
The Prophet ﷺ entered, circled the House, prayed there and went home.
Al-Bukhārī reports that after Badr the Prophet ﷺ said that if al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī were alive and had spoken to him about the captives, he would have let them go for his sake.
Ḥirāʾ is about 5 km north-east of the Kaʿba in a straight line, close enough to send messages into the town.

people.name: al-Muṭʿim b. ʿAdī
people.who: Chief of Banū Nawfal, one of the five who ended the boycott; died before Badr without becoming Muslim
people.here: Took the Prophet under his protection

people.name: Ḥassān b. Thābit
people.who: Poet of the Anṣār
people.here: His elegy for al-Muṭʿim preserves the memory

reveal.text: The armed escort went to the Mosque first and only then sent word for him to come in.

question.q: The Prophet ﷺ could re-enter his own city only on the guarantee of a non-Muslim chief, after two others refused. What does this say about his position in Makkah by 619?

options.text: He had no standing of his own left in Makkah; he lived there on another man's word
options.why: Two refusals and an armed escort show how exposed he was.

options.text: Makkah could no longer be the base for the call; a new home with real protection was needed
options.why: The next act turns to the tribes at the pilgrimage seasons in search of exactly that.

units.matters: This is where the act ends: the Prophet ﷺ in his birthplace on borrowed protection. Every later step, from the tribes at the fairs to Yathrib, is a search for a people who would protect him as their own.
